current_law_statement: Researched 2026-08-19 against the codified Government Code on leginfo.legislature.ca.gov (CPRA as recodified by AB 473, Stats. 2021, ch. 614, operative Jan. 1, 2023). Sessions reviewed: 2023-24 (SB 1034 — § 7922.535 state-of-emergency extension; SB 1525 — § 7922.525 technical) and 2025-26 (AB 370, Stats. 2025, ch. 34 — § 7922.535 cyberattack extension, eff. Jan. 1, 2026; SB 707, Stats. 2025, ch. 327 — Brown Act incl. § 54953.5; AB 1821 — pending, fee/commercial provisions struck 06/25/26, now amends only § 7922.535, on Senate third reading 08/19/26, NOT law). The fee provisions themselves — §§ 7922.530(a)-(b) and 7922.575(a)-(b) — are unamended since AB 473 (they carry forward former §§ 6253(b) and 6253.9 without substantive change). No administrative rule or uniform fee schedule implements CPRA fees; the AG's 2004 CPRA Summary is no longer hosted (404), so the only official guidance opened is AG Op. No. 04-1105 (2005). Controlling case law: National Lawyers Guild v. City of Hayward (2020) 9 Cal.5th 488 (opened, courts.ca.gov archive PDF). Municipal scope: every CPRA fee rule binds 'each state or local agency' identically; Brown Act and § 6159 rows add municipal-specific texture; counties' § 54985 authority is noted and excluded.

resolutions.unit: USD per page (city sets under the standard)
resolutions.source_language: Except with respect to public records exempt from disclosure by express provisions of law, each state or local agency, upon a request for a copy of records that reasonably describes an identifiable record or records, shall make the records promptly available to any person upon payment of fees covering direct costs of duplication, or a statutory fee if applicable. Upon request, an exact copy shall be provided unless impracticable to do so.
resolutions.effective_status: Current (added Stats. 2021, ch. 614 (AB 473), operative Jan. 1, 2023; no amendment 2024–2026 as of 2026-08-19)
resolutions.notes: No statewide cents-per-page figure for general municipal records; the standard is 'direct costs of duplication' (judicially glossed as the cost of running the copy machine and conceivably the operator, excluding retrieval/inspection/handling — CA-9003). 'Or a statutory fee if applicable' points to record-specific statutes; the only general-application one binding city clerks found is Gov. Code § 81008 (Political Reform Act statements ≤ $0.10/page, CA-9009). Counties (not cities) have separate authority under Gov. Code § 54985 to set copy fees at reasonable cost per 85 Ops.Cal.Atty.Gen. 225 (2002) (located, not opened). Applies to 'each state or local agency' — no separate state-agency schedule.

resolutions.source_language: But the term “extraction” does not cover every process that might be colloquially described as “taking information out.” It does not, for example, cover time spent searching for responsive records in an e-mail inbox or a computer’s documents folder. Just as agencies cannot recover the costs of searching through a filing cabinet for paper records, they cannot recover comparable costs for electronic records. Nor, for similar reasons, does “extraction” cover the cost of redacting exempt data from otherwise producible electronic records.
resolutions.effective_status: Current (published opinion, May 28, 2020; construes former § 6253.9(b)(2), continued without substantive change as § 7922.575(b))
resolutions.notes: Search/retrieval staff time is categorically non-chargeable for paper records ('direct costs of duplication' excludes retrieval — North County Parents as quoted in NLG, CA-9003) and for electronic records (NLG: searching an e-mail inbox or documents folder is not 'extraction'). The only labor a requester bears is § 7922.575(b) construction/programming/extraction (see labor.programming.rate). Opinion cites pre-recodification section numbers.

new_rules.legal_concept: No charge for requester's own-equipment copying during on-premises inspection
new_rules.atomic_rule: A requester inspecting a disclosable record on the agency's premises may photograph or otherwise copy the record with the requester's own equipment without being charged any fees or costs, provided the method does not physically contact the record, damage it, or access the agency's systems; the agency may impose reasonable limits to protect the records or its orderly function.
new_rules.trigger: Requester inspects on premises and uses own equipment
new_rules.source_language: A requester who inspects a disclosable record on the premises of the agency has the right to use the requester’s equipment on those premises, without being charged any fees or costs, to photograph or otherwise copy or reproduce the record in a manner that does not require the equipment to make physical contact with the record, unless the means of copy or reproduction would result in either of the following: (1) Damage to the record. (2) Unauthorized access to the agency’s computer systems or secured networks by using software, equipment, or any other technology capable of accessing, altering, or compromising the agency’s electronic records.
new_rules.effective_status: Current (added Stats. 2021, ch. 614 (AB 473), operative Jan. 1, 2023; no amendment 2024–2026 as of 2026-08-19)
new_rules.notes: applies_to: all_public_bodies ('the agency' — state or local). Bears on rules.freePages (no per-page allowance, but self-copying is free). Subdivision (c) limits are structural, not a value.

new_rules.legal_concept: Redaction and search of electronic records not chargeable as 'data extraction'
new_rules.atomic_rule: An agency may not charge a requester for the cost of redacting exempt material from otherwise disclosable electronic records (including digital video footage), nor for time spent searching for responsive electronic records; such tasks are not 'data compilation, extraction, or programming' under § 7922.575(b) (former § 6253.9(b)(2)).
new_rules.trigger: Request for electronic records requiring search or redaction
new_rules.source_language: We hold only that section 6253.9(b)(2), as presently written, does not provide a basis for charging requesters for the costs of redacting government records kept in an electronic format, including digital video footage. … But the term “extraction” does not cover every process that might be colloquially described as “taking information out.” It does not, for example, cover time spent searching for responsive records in an e-mail inbox or a computer’s documents folder. Just as agencies cannot recover the costs of searching through a filing cabinet for paper records, they cannot recover comparable costs for electronic records. Nor, for similar reasons, does “extraction” cover the cost of redacting exempt data from otherwise producible electronic records.
new_rules.source_authority: National Lawyers Guild, S.F. Bay Area Chapter v. City of Hayward (2020) 9 Cal.5th 488 (Cal. Supreme Court, No. S252445, May 28, 2020)
new_rules.effective_status: Current (published May 28, 2020; construes former § 6253.9(b)(2), recodified without substantive change as § 7922.575(b) by Stats. 2021, ch. 614)
new_rules.notes: AMENDS CA-0024: replaces its is_paraphrase=true holding text with the verbatim holding and the searching/redaction passage from the opened official opinion (courts.ca.gov archive PDF, pp. 25 & 28). Also disapproves Fredericks v. Superior Court (2015) 233 Cal.App.4th 209 to the extent inconsistent. applies_to: all_public_bodies.

new_rules.legal_concept: 'Direct costs of duplication' excludes retrieval, inspection, review and redaction time
new_rules.atomic_rule: 'Direct costs of duplication' covers the cost of running the copy machine and conceivably the expense of the person operating it, and excludes the ancillary tasks of retrieval, inspection and handling of the file, including staff time searching the records, reviewing them for exempt information, and deleting exempt information.
new_rules.trigger: Any request for copies of paper records
new_rules.source_language: The reference to “direct costs of duplication” has long been understood to cover “the ‘cost of running the copy machine, and conceivably also the expense of the person operating it’ while excluding any charge for ‘the ancillary tasks necessarily associated with the retrieval, inspection and handling of the file from which the copy is extracted.’ ” (County of Santa Clara, supra, 170 Cal.App.4th at p. 1336, quoting North County Parents Organization v. Department of Education (1994) 23 Cal.App.4th 144, 148 (North County).) Nonchargeable ancillary costs include “staff time involved in searching the records, reviewing records for information exempt from disclosure under law, and deleting such exempt information.” (North County, at p. 146.)
new_rules.source_authority: National Lawyers Guild, S.F. Bay Area Chapter v. City of Hayward (2020) 9 Cal.5th 488 (Cal. Supreme Court, No. S252445, May 28, 2020), at 9 Cal.5th pp. 3-4 of slip op., quoting County of Santa Clara v. Superior Court (2009) 170 Cal.App.4th 1301, 1336 and North County Parents Organization v. Department of Education (1994) 23 Cal.App.4th 144, 146, 148
new_rules.effective_status: Current (statement of settled construction of former § 6257/§ 6253(b), now § 7922.530(a))
new_rules.notes: Verbatim from the opened NLG opinion; the North County and County of Santa Clara opinions themselves were not opened (official reporter not freely hosted) — the quotation is as reproduced by the Supreme Court. applies_to: all_public_bodies. Resolves labor.search.rate / labor.review.rate as not_applicable.

new_rules.legal_concept: § 7922.575(b) cost-shift excludes initial gathering, conversion and maintenance costs
new_rules.atomic_rule: When the § 7922.575(b) cost-shift applies, the fee may include the cost to construct the record and the cost of programming and computer services necessary to produce a copy, but may not include expenses associated with the agency's initial gathering of the information, its initial conversion into an electronic format, or its maintenance.
new_rules.trigger: Electronic record produced only at scheduled intervals, or request requires data compilation/extraction/programming
new_rules.source_language: If the request is made at a time other than when the data is periodically produced, the fee may additionally include “the cost to construct [the] record, and the cost of programming and computer services necessary to produce a copy of the record.” (§ 6253.9, subd. (b)(1).) The fee may similarly cover such additional costs when “[t]he request would require data compilation, extraction, or programming to produce the record.” (§ 6253.9, subd. (b)(2).) In either event, however, the fee may not include expenses associated with the county’s initial gathering of the information, or with initial conversion of the information into an electronic format, or with maintaining the information.
new_rules.source_authority: Cal. Atty. Gen. Op. No. 04-1105 (Oct. 3, 2005) (Lockyer, A.G.; Stone, D.A.G.), Conclusion 3 and Analysis pt. 3 (reported at 88 Ops.Cal.Atty.Gen. 153 — reporter cite to be verified)
new_rules.notes: Question posed about a county assessor's parcel-map data; the reasoning construes the statute generally ('a state or local agency'). applies_to: all_public_bodies (opinion addressed to counties). Bears on labor.programming.rate, dup.specialty.rate, labor.overheadPct.

new_rules.legal_concept: Local legislative body may charge a fee or deposit for copies; no disability surcharge
new_rules.atomic_rule: The Brown Act does not prevent the legislative body of a local agency from charging a fee or deposit for a copy of a public record pursuant to § 7922.530, except that no surcharge may be imposed on persons with disabilities in violation of ADA Title II.
new_rules.trigger: Local agency charges for a copy of a public record (agenda materials or otherwise)
new_rules.source_language: This chapter shall not be construed to prevent the legislative body of a local agency from charging a fee or deposit for a copy of a public record pursuant to Section 7922.530, except that a surcharge shall not be imposed on persons with disabilities in violation of Section 202 of the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990 (42 U.S.C. Sec. 12132), and the federal rules and regulations adopted in implementation thereof.
new_rules.source_authority: Cal. Gov. Code § 54957.5(d) (Ralph M. Brown Act)
new_rules.notes: applies_to: municipalities (local agencies; the Brown Act does not govern state agencies). Non-preclusion clause — it presupposes rather than grants deposit authority; no threshold or cap. Basis for rules.deposit.threshold = defers_to_city. The ADA no-surcharge clause is a Prohibition rider (secondary rule type).

new_rules.legal_concept: City may accept credit/debit card or electronic funds transfer for fees, with city council approval
new_rules.atomic_rule: A city (or county, city and county, or other public agency) may authorize acceptance of a credit card, debit card, or electronic funds transfer for payment of services rendered or any fee or charge due the agency; a city must obtain its city council's approval, and any other public agency the approval of its fiscally responsible governing body.
new_rules.trigger: Agency elects to accept electronic payment
new_rules.source_language: Subject to subdivisions (c) and (d), a court, city, county, city and county, or other public agency may authorize the acceptance of a credit card, debit card, or electronic funds transfer for any of the following: … (5) The payment for services rendered by a city, county, city and county, or other public agency. (6) The payment of a fee, charge, or tax due a city, county, city and county, or other public agency. … A city desiring to authorize the use of a credit card, debit card, or electronic funds transfer pursuant to subdivision (b) shall obtain the approval of its city council. Any other public agency desiring to authorize the use of a credit card, debit card, or electronic funds transfer pursuant to subdivision (b) shall obtain the approval of the governing body that has fiscal responsibility for that agency.
new_rules.notes: General local-finance statute, not CPRA-specific; the ellipsis omits paragraphs (1)-(4), (7)-(8) (bail, court fees, towing, support, sheriff levies, county gifts). applies_to: all_public_bodies (cities named expressly). Resolves payment.method as defers_to_city.

new_rules.legal_concept: Card/EFT convenience fee capped at the agency's cost, governing-body approved
new_rules.atomic_rule: A city or other public agency may impose a fee for the use of a credit or debit card or electronic funds transfer not to exceed the costs incurred by the agency in providing for that payment method (including card-issuer fees or discounts), and the fee must be approved by the governing body responsible for the agency's fiscal decisions.
new_rules.trigger: Agency accepts card/EFT payment and elects to pass through processing cost
new_rules.source_language: Notwithstanding Title 1.3 (commencing with Section 1747) of Part 4 of Division 3 of the Civil Code, a court or agent of the court, city, county, city and county, or any other public agency may impose a fee for the use of a credit or debit card or electronic funds transfer, not to exceed the costs incurred by the agency or agent in providing for payment by credit or debit card or electronic funds transfer. These costs may include, but shall not be limited to, the payment of fees or discounts as specified in paragraph (3) of subdivision (d). A fee imposed by a court or agent of the court pursuant to this subdivision shall be approved by the Judicial Council. A fee imposed by any other public agency pursuant to this subdivision for the use of a credit or debit card or electronic funds transfer shall be approved by the governing body responsible for the fiscal decisions of the public agency.
new_rules.notes: ceiling: costs incurred in providing card/EFT payment. Subdivision (g) separately allows a returned-payment charge not to exceed actual costs. applies_to: all_public_bodies.

new_rules.legal_concept: Agency may adopt requirements allowing greater access than the CPRA minimums (basis for local fee reduction/waiver policy)
new_rules.atomic_rule: Except as otherwise prohibited by law, a state or local agency may adopt requirements for itself that allow for faster, more efficient, or greater access to records than the CPRA's minimum standards.
new_rules.trigger: Agency adopts its own records policy (including charging less than direct cost or waiving fees)
new_rules.source_language: Except as otherwise prohibited by law, a state or local agency may adopt requirements for itself that allow for faster, more efficient, or greater access to records than prescribed by the minimum standards set forth in this division.
new_rules.effective_status: Current (added Stats. 2021, ch. 614 (AB 473), operative Jan. 1, 2023; no amendment 2024–2026 as of 2026-08-19)
new_rules.notes: Mapped to fee.waiver only because it is the sole statutory hook for a local waiver policy; the clause is general and not fee-specific (flag for the reconcile step — may better sit under a general 'agency may exceed minimums' key if the dictionary has one). applies_to: all_public_bodies.

new_rules.legal_concept: Political Reform Act statements: copies ≤ $0.10/page; retrieval fee ≤ $5/request for records 5+ years old
new_rules.atomic_rule: A filing officer (including a city clerk) shall provide copies of reports and statements filed under the Political Reform Act at a charge not to exceed ten cents ($0.10) per page, and may charge a retrieval fee not to exceed five dollars ($5) per request for copies of reports and statements five or more years old; a request for several reports/statements at one time is a single request.
new_rules.trigger: Request for copies of campaign statements / statements of economic interests filed under the Political Reform Act
new_rules.source_language: Copies shall be provided at a charge not to exceed ten cents ($0.10) per page. In addition, the filing officer may charge a retrieval fee not to exceed five dollars ($5) per request for copies of reports and statements which are five or more years old. A request for more than one report or statement or report and statement at the same time shall be considered a single request.
new_rules.source_authority: Cal. Gov. Code § 81008 (Political Reform Act; two codified versions — Stats. 2013, ch. 654 and Stats. 2018, ch. 662 (SB 1239, conditionally operative) — carry identical fee text)
new_rules.effective_status: Current (fee text identical in both codified versions; the SB 1239 version's operative date is tied to Secretary of State certification under Stats. 2018, ch. 662, § 44 — verify which is operative if precision matters)
new_rules.notes: This is the 'statutory fee if applicable' path from § 7922.530(a) for one common municipal record class (city clerks are PRA filing officers). ceiling: $0.10/page; retrieval $5/request (5+ years old). No conditions or identification may be imposed on requesters. applies_to: all_public_bodies (all filing officers).

new_rules.legal_concept: Agenda-packet mailing fee may not exceed the cost of providing the service
new_rules.atomic_rule: The legislative body of a local agency may establish a fee for mailing the agenda or agenda packet to a person who has requested it, which fee shall not exceed the cost of providing the service; e-mail delivery must be provided on request where the agency has a website.
new_rules.trigger: Standing request for mailed agenda/agenda packet
new_rules.source_language: The legislative body may establish a fee for mailing the agenda or agenda packet, which fee shall not exceed the cost of providing the service.
new_rules.source_authority: Cal. Gov. Code § 54954.1 (Ralph M. Brown Act)
new_rules.notes: Record-specific (agenda materials) and local-agency only; the CPRA itself has no postage/handling rule. applies_to: municipalities.

new_rules.legal_concept: Inspection of meeting audio/video recordings free on agency equipment
new_rules.atomic_rule: Any inspection of a local agency's audio or video recording of an open meeting shall be provided without charge on equipment made available by the local agency; the recording is subject to CPRA inspection and may be erased 30 days after the recording notwithstanding § 34090.
new_rules.trigger: Request to inspect a recording of a legislative-body meeting
new_rules.source_language: Any recording of an open and public meeting made for whatever purpose by or at the direction of the local agency shall be subject to inspection pursuant to the California Public Records Act (Division 10 (commencing with Section 7920.000) of Title 1), but, notwithstanding Section 34090, may be erased or destroyed 30 days after the recording. Any inspection of an audio or video recording shall be provided without charge on equipment made available by the local agency.
new_rules.source_authority: Cal. Gov. Code § 54953.5(b) (Ralph M. Brown Act)
new_rules.notes: Inspection-only no-charge rule; copies of the recording remain subject to the § 7922.575(a) direct-cost standard. applies_to: municipalities. applicability_notes: All CPRA fee provisions (§§ 7922.530, 7922.575) bind 'each state or local agency' alike — California has no separate state-agency uniform fee schedule and no local-body regime distinct from the state regime; every statutory resolution here is applies_to=all_public_bodies.

Counties (not cities) hold separate fee authority under Gov. Code § 54985(a) (board of supervisors may set fees at cost reasonably necessary, including OMB A-87 indirect costs); 85 Ops.Cal.Atty.Gen. 225 (2002) reads it to allow county copy fees above 'direct costs of duplication'. Located by index only, not opened; excluded as county-only. Do not extend to municipalities.

Brown Act rows (CA-9005 § 54957.5(d), CA-9010 § 54954.1, CA-9012 § 54953.5(b)) bind local agencies (cities, counties, districts) — applies_to=municipalities; state bodies are under the Bagley-Keene Act instead.
Gov. Code § 6159 (CA-9006/9007) names cities expressly and 'other public agency'; treated as all_public_bodies. Its convenience-fee ceiling is 'costs incurred', a soft ceiling the city quantifies.

Cal. Const. art. XIII C § 1(e)(2) (Prop. 26) independently caps any local-government service charge at 'the reasonable costs to the local government of providing the service or product' — a municipal-only backstop that is looser than the CPRA's direct-cost standard and therefore never the operative ceiling for copy fees; recorded here as context, not as a rule row.

Gov. Code § 81008 (CA-9009) binds every Political Reform Act filing officer, including city clerks; it is record-specific and is the only concrete cents-per-page ceiling found that reaches municipalities.
The NLG v. Hayward and AG 04-1105 rows construe the statute generally; the parties were a city and a county respectively, and nothing in either limits the holding by agency type.
material_negatives: No statewide per-page copy rate for general municipal records (B&W, color, oversized, specialty) — only the 'direct costs of duplication' standard (§ 7922.530(a)).

No fee-estimate/cost-notice duty at any threshold; no requester response window, revision-percentage or estimate-validity rule (the § 7922.535(a) 'estimate' is a date/time of availability, not a cost).

No deposit threshold, deposit cap, nonpayment-withdrawal, deposit-clock, or overrun re-issue rule in the CPRA; the only mention of a 'deposit' for copies is the Brown Act's non-preclusion clause (§ 54957.5(d)).

No labor charging at all for search, review, or redaction — paper or electronic (North County Parents via NLG; NLG v. Hayward); the sole cost-shift is § 7922.575(b) construction/programming/extraction, with no rate, increment, overhead, or free-hours rule.
No commercial-purpose schedule, no fee-waiver provision (grounds, mandatory/discretionary, purpose statement, written denial, appeal), no fee forfeiture for late response, no repeat/aggregation rule.
No de-minimis, minimum-fee, certification-fee (general), delivery/postage, or per-minute audio/video rule.
No administrative rule, uniform fee schedule, or AG rule implements CPRA fees; the AG's 2004 CPRA Summary is no longer hosted (oag.ca.gov returns 404).

AB 1821 (2025-26): the fee/commercial-use/aggregation provisions were struck by the 06/25/26 Senate amendment; as of 2026-08-19 the bill amends only § 7922.535 (business days), is on Senate third reading, and is not law.
